blockMcqs.question: What do all creational patterns have in common?
options: They define how objects communicate
They control how objects get created
They add new behavior to existing objects
They manage object destruction only
blockMcqs.explanation: Creational patterns hide the details of object construction behind a clean interface.

blockMcqs.question: What problem does Singleton solve?
options: Building families of related objects
Ensuring only one instance of a class exists
Cloning expensive objects cheaply
Letting subclasses choose a type
blockMcqs.explanation: Singleton guarantees exactly one instance and a single global access point to it.

blockMcqs.question: In the Singleton pseudocode, why is the constructor private?
options: To speed up construction
To stop outside code from creating extra instances
Because private methods run faster
To allow multiple subclasses
blockMcqs.explanation: A private constructor forces all access through getInstance(), which controls the single instance.

blockMcqs.question: In Factory Method, who decides the concrete class to create?
options: The client calling the method
A subclass overriding the factory method
The abstract base class always
A separate cloning routine
blockMcqs.explanation: Factory Method lets subclasses override the creation step to pick the concrete type.

blockMcqs.question: When is Abstract Factory the right choice?
options: When only one object is ever created
When related objects must be created as a matching family
When cloning is cheaper than building
When no interfaces are involved
blockMcqs.explanation: Abstract Factory keeps a whole family of related products consistent, like matching UI themes.

blockMcqs.question: In the UI factory pseudocode, what does swapping DarkUiFactory for LightUiFactory change?
options: Nothing, factories are interchangeable no-ops
The entire family of components produced
Only the button, never the checkbox
The interface each component implements
blockMcqs.explanation: Swapping the factory instance swaps the whole matching family of products it creates.

blockMcqs.question: What problem does the Builder pattern mainly address?
options: Too many subclasses of one interface
Constructors needing many optional parameters
Needing exactly one shared instance
Copying objects instead of building them
blockMcqs.explanation: Builder replaces long or telescoping constructors with clear, chainable step-by-step setup.

blockMcqs.question: Prototype is most useful when:
options: Every object must be unique and uncopyable
Building a new object from scratch is expensive
Only one instance should ever exist
Objects need no internal state
blockMcqs.explanation: Prototype clones an existing instance to avoid repeating costly construction work.

blockMcqs.question: In the Enemy clone() pseudocode, why deep-copy the stats object?
options: Deep copy is always faster
So clones don't share and corrupt the same mutable state
Shallow copy is not allowed in Prototype
It avoids implementing an interface
blockMcqs.explanation: A shallow copy would let two clones share one stats object, so editing one affects the other.

blockMcqs.question: Why is Singleton overuse considered risky?
options: It makes objects impossible to clone
It introduces hidden global state and hurts testability
It forces every class to be abstract
It prevents families of related objects
blockMcqs.explanation: Overused Singletons act as global mutable state, hiding dependencies and complicating isolated tests.
